# South African Government Reshuffles as Mbeki Steps Down

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa (CNN)** — Ten South African ministers and the deputy president have tendered their resignations as President Thabo Mbeki prepares to depart office. Mbeki formally announced his resignation during a televised address on Sunday, paving the way for African National Congress Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe to be sworn in as the nation's new president on Thursday.

Mbeki's announcement prompted several Cabinet members to threaten resignation as well, though the outgoing president urged them to remain in their posts, according to government sources. Nonetheless, a government statement confirmed that the resignations—including those of Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota—will take effect Thursday, coinciding with Mbeki's departure. "All the ministers have expressed their availability to assist the incoming administration in the hand-over process and any other assistance that might be sought from them," the statement noted. A representative for Manuel told CNN that the finance minister remains willing to serve in the new government should his services be required. Three deputy ministers have also submitted their resignations.

An ANC spokesman confirmed that the party has designated Motlanthe as Mbeki's successor. He will serve until national elections next spring, in which ANC President Jacob Zuma is widely favored to prevail.

Earlier this month, the ANC called on Mbeki to resign after a judge dismissed corruption, fraud, and racketeering charges against Zuma—Mbeki's longtime political rival—ruling the case invalid and accusing Mbeki's administration of political interference.

During his resignation address, Mbeki—who has led South Africa for nearly a decade—reflected on his tenure's achievements. "I depart this office knowing that many men and women in South Africa have worked to achieve better lives for all," he said, noting that the country experienced its longest sustained period of economic growth in its history under his leadership, alongside unprecedented outreach to impoverished communities. He acknowledged that South Africa still faces significant challenges in economic development, corruption, and crime, and expressed confidence in the incoming leadership without naming a specific successor.

Gwede Mantashe, the ANC's secretary-general, announced Saturday that the party—which Mbeki has belonged to since his youth—had requested his early departure, a request to which Mbeki consented. Mantashe explained that the decision was made "for the citizens of South Africa, so there could be stability within the country," and to preserve unity within the ANC.

The corruption case against Zuma, who succeeded Mbeki as ANC president last year, was initially dismissed in September 2006, though the National Prosecuting Authority subsequently refiled charges. Judge Chris Nicholson's recent ruling made no determination regarding Zuma's guilt or innocence, leaving open the possibility of renewed prosecution—though political observers consider this unlikely given Zuma's substantial popular support, particularly among the Communist Party and trade unions. Zuma has consistently denied the allegations, characterizing the case as politically motivated and detrimental to his candidacy for the ANC presidency. Had he been convicted of accepting bribes connected to a multibillion-dollar arms deal, he could have faced a minimum 15-year prison sentence. He also faced allegations of maintaining a corrupt relationship with his former financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, who is currently serving 15 years for soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf and leveraging Zuma's political influence for personal business gain.

Mbeki, 66, succeeded Nelson Mandela as South Africa's president in June 1999. Critics have alleged that he was instrumental in pursuing the corruption charges against Zuma. Notably, Mbeki recently brokered a landmark power-sharing agreement between Zimbabwe's rival political factions, signed Monday in an effort to move beyond a violent past and resolve the crisis that has gripped Zimbabwe since the disputed national elections in March. Under the agreement, longtime leader Robert Mugabe retains the presidency, while his longstanding rival, Morgan Tsvangirai, assumes the role of prime minister overseeing government affairs.

# South African Political Crisis: Mass Resignations Follow Mbeki's Departure

South Africa was thrown into a period of significant political transition this week as ten government ministers, including Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, tendered their resignations alongside the deputy president, all stepping down in the wake of President Thabo Mbeki's own departure from office.

## Mbeki's Farewell Address

President Mbeki formally announced his resignation during a televised address to the nation on Sunday. In his remarks, he took time to reflect on the achievements of his administration, looking back over nearly a decade of leadership. The speech marked the end of an era for South African politics, as Mbeki had been a central figure in the country's post-apartheid governance since taking office in 1999.

## A New Leader Emerges

In the aftermath of Mbeki's resignation, ANC Deputy President Kgalema Motlanthe was named as his successor. Motlanthe is set to be sworn in as South Africa's new president on Thursday, and he will serve in this capacity until national elections are held in the spring of the following year. His appointment represents a transitional leadership arrangement designed to steady the government during this politically sensitive period.

## Cabinet Resignations and the Question of Continuity

The wave of ministerial resignations was a direct response to Mbeki's exit, even though the outgoing president had specifically urged members of his Cabinet to remain in their positions. Despite stepping down, the ministers—including key figures overseeing finance and defense—expressed their willingness to continue assisting the incoming administration throughout the transition period, signaling an effort to maintain governmental stability despite the upheaval at the top.

## The Roots of the Crisis: Zuma, Corruption, and Political Interference

The chain of events leading to Mbeki's resignation can be traced back to mounting pressure from within the African National Congress (ANC) itself. This pressure intensified after a judge dismissed the corruption case against ANC President Jacob Zuma, Mbeki's political rival. In dismissing the charges, the judge leveled serious accusations against Mbeki's government, alleging political interference in the prosecution of Zuma. This ruling effectively undermined Mbeki's position within the party and accelerated calls for his removal, ultimately culminating in his resignation as head of state and the subsequent cascade of Cabinet departures that followed.

South Africa is undergoing a dramatic political transition following the resignation of President Thabo Mbeki, a move that has sent shockwaves through the nation's government and exposed deep fractures within the ruling African National Congress (ANC). Mbeki's departure came in the wake of a dismissed corruption case against his long-time political rival, Jacob Zuma, a decision that intensified tensions between the two factions of the party and ultimately forced the president's hand.

In a striking display of solidarity—or perhaps strategic repositioning ahead of the transition—ten government ministers have followed Mbeki's lead and tendered their resignations. Among those stepping down are some of the most prominent figures in Mbeki's cabinet, including Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, whose economic stewardship had been widely credited with maintaining investor confidence in South Africa, and Defense Minister Mosiuoa Lekota, a veteran ANC figure with deep roots in the anti-apartheid struggle. The deputy president has also resigned as part of this broader reshuffling, signaling that the transition extends well beyond the presidency itself and into the highest echelons of government.

The mass resignations reflect the loyalty many of these officials felt toward Mbeki, as well as uncertainty about their roles under the incoming administration. Whether these departures represent a coordinated protest against the manner of Mbeki's removal or simply pragmatic preparation for a change in leadership remains a subject of debate among political analysts.

Stepping into the breach is Kgalema Motlanthe, a senior ANC official who is set to be sworn in as South Africa's new president this Thursday. Motlanthe's tenure, however, is widely understood to be a caretaker arrangement rather than a long-term mandate. He is expected to serve only until national elections are held in the spring, at which point Jacob Zuma—having emerged victorious in the ANC's internal leadership battle and now cleared of legal jeopardy following the dismissal of his corruption case—is widely anticipated to secure the presidency in his own right through the ballot box.

This chain of events marks one of the most significant political transitions South Africa has experienced since the end of apartheid, underscoring the deep internal divisions that have emerged within the ANC. The party, which has dominated South African politics for over a decade, now finds itself navigating a delicate period of transition, with the outcome likely to shape the country's governance and economic policy direction for years to come. # Johannesburg: The City of Gold

Johannesburg, often called "Jozi" or "Egoli" (City of Gold), stands as South Africa's largest city and the economic powerhouse of the African continent. Founded in 1886 following the discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand, the city grew rapidly from a mining camp into a sprawling metropolis that would shape the nation's history.

Unlike many South African cities, Johannesburg was not built around a natural harbor or river but around mineral wealth, making it a unique urban phenomenon born purely from industrial ambition. This gold rush heritage is still visible today in the mine dumps that dot the landscape and in the city's continued role as a global center for gold and diamond trading.

Johannesburg played a pivotal role during the apartheid era, particularly through townships like Soweto (South Western Townships), which became a center of resistance against racial segregation. The Soweto Uprising of 1976 marked a turning point in the struggle against apartheid, drawing international attention to South Africa's oppressive policies.

Today, Johannesburg is a vibrant, multicultural city that serves as the financial and commercial hub of South Africa. It hosts the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, one of the largest in Africa, and numerous multinational corporations have established their African headquarters here. The city's population reflects incredible diversity, with people from across South Africa and the broader African continent contributing to its dynamic culture.

Districts like Maboneng and Braamfontein showcase urban renewal efforts, featuring art galleries, trendy restaurants, and creative spaces that have emerged from previously neglected areas. The Apartheid Museum and Constitution Hill offer visitors profound insights into South Africa's complex history and its journey toward democracy.

Despite challenges including inequality and crime rates that persist as legacies of its turbulent past, Johannesburg continues to reinvent itself as a symbol of resilience, embodying both the struggles and triumphs of modern South Africa.

# Mbeki Resigns as South African President Amid ANC Power Struggle; Cabinet Exodus Follows

**JOHANNESBURG, South Africa** — President Thabo Mbeki announced his resignation Sunday night in a televised address to the nation, bowing to pressure from his own African National Congress party following a court ruling that suggested he had improperly interfered in corruption charges against his political rival, Jacob Zuma.

The resignation, effective within days, throws South African politics into a period of uncertainty and marks a stunning fall for a leader who had guided Africa's largest economy for nearly a decade.

"I have therefore tendered my resignation as president of the Republic of South Africa," Mbeki told the nation in a solemn address from the Union Buildings in Pretoria. "I have taken this decision in the interest of the unity of our movement and the stability of our young democracy."

## A Bitter Party Feud

Mbeki's departure caps months of escalating tension within the ANC, culminating in a ruling by a Pietermaritzburg High Court judge who found that Mbeki's government may have used the National Prosecuting Authority to pursue corruption charges against Zuma for political purposes. The ruling threw out the corruption case against Zuma but also inflicted a devastating political blow on Mbeki.

The ANC's national executive committee, now firmly under the control of Zuma loyalists after Mbeki lost the party presidency to his rival at a bruising conference in Polokwane late last year, voted to formally recall Mbeki from the presidency — an extraordinary move that left him little choice but to step down.

Analysts described the schism as the most serious threat to ANC unity since the end of apartheid, pitting Mbeki's technocratic, market-friendly wing of the party against Zuma's populist coalition of trade unionists, communists and youth league firebrands.

## Cabinet Ministers Follow Him Out

In a dramatic show of solidarity, at least ten Cabinet ministers and several deputy ministers submitted their resignations in the hours following Mbeki's announcement, according to sources within the presidency.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, widely credited with stewarding South Africa's post-apartheid economic growth and maintaining investor confidence, was among those who tendered his resignation, sending brief tremors through South African financial markets Monday morning. The rand slipped against the dollar in early trading before steadying.

Other ministers who resigned included those overseeing safety and security, foreign affairs, and public enterprises — raising immediate questions about continuity of governance during the transition.

Party officials moved quickly to project calm, with ANC Secretary-General Gwede Mantashe insisting the resignations were a personal show of loyalty to Mbeki rather than a rejection of the party's new leadership, and expressing confidence that a new Cabinet would be sworn in without disruption to state functions.

## What Happens Next

Under South Africa's constitution, Parliament is expected to convene this week to elect a caretaker president to serve out the remainder of Mbeki's term, which was due to end with elections in 2009. Deputy President Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka's own position is now unclear following the Cabinet resignations, and speculation in Cape Town has centered on Kgalema Motlanthe, the ANC's deputy president, as the most likely interim head of state.

Zuma himself is not eligible to assume the presidency immediately, as he holds no seat in Parliament, but he is widely expected to lead the ANC into next year's general election and become president following that vote — despite corruption allegations that have dogged him for years and could yet resurface.

## International Reaction

The resignation sent ripples through international markets and diplomatic circles. Mbeki had been a central figure on the African continent, serving as a mediator in conflicts from Zimbabwe to Côte d'Ivoire, and his sudden departure raises questions about the continuity of those diplomatic efforts, particularly ongoing power-sharing negotiations between Zimbabwe's Robert Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai.

The Congress of South African Trade Unions and the South African Communist Party, both key allies in the coalition that helped oust Mbeki, welcomed the resignation, with COSATU calling it "a victory for internal democracy" within the ANC.

Opposition parties, however, voiced alarm. Helen Zille, leader of the Democratic Alliance, called the events "a deeply troubling display of a ruling party placing its own factional battles above the interests of the country," and called for early elections.

Mbeki, 66, leaves office having presided over years of robust economic growth and an expanding black middle class, though his legacy remains contested — critics point to his government's widely criticized handling of the HIV/AIDS epidemic and his quiet diplomacy toward Zimbabwe as significant blemishes on his tenure.

He has not indicated his plans following his departure from office.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Mbeki Resigns as South African President Amid ANC Recall

**Johannesburg** — Thabo Mbeki formally resigned as President of South Africa on September 21, 2008, following a decision by the African National Congress (ANC) to recall him from office—a dramatic end to a presidency that had steered the country since 1999.

## The ANC's Decision to Recall

The ANC's National Executive Committee (NEC) voted to recall Mbeki after a High Court ruling raised serious questions about his conduct toward Jacob Zuma, the ANC's own party president. Party officials argued that Mbeki could no longer effectively serve as head of state given the implications of the ruling, and the NEC concluded that his continued presence in the Union Buildings undermined party unity and public confidence in the government. The recall marked an extraordinary rebuke from the very party that had once been his political home base, exposing deep factional rifts within the ANC that had been simmering since Zuma's election as ANC president at the Polokwane conference in December 2007.

## Background: The Jacob Zuma Corruption Trial

At the heart of the controversy was a long-running corruption and racketeering case against Zuma, stemming from a multi-billion-rand arms deal in the late 1990s. Zuma had been dismissed as Deputy President by Mbeki in 2005 after his financial adviser, Schabir Shaik, was convicted of soliciting bribes on Zuma's behalf. Zuma always maintained his innocence, framing the prosecution as a politically motivated attempt to derail his rise within the ANC.

The pivotal moment came when Judge Chris Nicholson, ruling in the Durban High Court, found procedural flaws in the timing and handling of the charges against Zuma. Crucially, the judge suggested there may have been political interference by the Mbeki administration in the prosecutorial process—an allegation Mbeki's office strenuously denied, but one that gave the ANC's leadership the pretext it needed to act.

## Kgalema Motlanthe Steps In

Following Mbeki's resignation, Parliament moved swiftly to elect Kgalema Motlanthe, then Deputy President of the ANC, as interim President of South Africa. Motlanthe, widely regarded as a unifying and steady figure within the party, was sworn in to serve out the remainder of the term ahead of the 2009 general elections. His appointment was seen as a caretaker measure, providing stability while the ANC prepared to install Zuma as president following the election.
